writing.prompt: Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay on why students should be encouraged to develop the ability to meet challenges. You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words.
writing.sample: In an era of rapid change, students inevitably encounter difficulties in their studies, career hunting and daily life. It is therefore of great importance that they be encouraged to develop the ability to meet challenges. There are several convincing reasons why this ability deserves cultivation. To begin with, facing challenges pushes students to unlock their hidden potential. A first-year student who dares to tackle a tough research project, for instance, often discovers strengths he never knew he possessed. More importantly, meeting challenges sharpens one's resilience and problem-solving skills. Every setback in a competition or an internship teaches valuable lessons that no textbook can offer. As a result, such students grow into independent thinkers who refuse to give up easily. In conclusion, since the ability to meet challenges prepares young people for fierce competition and lifelong growth, schools and families should spare no effort to foster it. Only by embracing challenges rather than avoiding them can students truly become masters of their own future.

transcript.en: M: Good morning, Safe House Insurance. My name is Paul. How can I help you today?
transcript.zh: M: 早上好，这里是 Safe House Insurance。我叫保罗。今天有什么可以帮您的吗？

transcript.en: W: Morning. I wouldn't say that it's good from where I am standing. This is Miss Wilson and this is the third time I've called this week since receiving your letter about our insurance claim. I'm getting a little fed up with my calls about my claim being completely disregarded.
transcript.zh: W: 早上好。从我的处境来看，我可不觉得这是个美好的早晨。我是威尔逊女士。自从收到你们关于我们保险理赔的信以来，这是我本周第三次打电话了。我对你们完全不理会我关于理赔的来电，已经有点受够了。

transcript.en: M: Miss Wilson, thank you for calling back. Can I take some details to help me look at your claim?
transcript.zh: M: 威尔逊女士，谢谢您再次来电。我可以先记录一些信息，以便查看您的理赔情况吗？

transcript.en: W: It's Miss May Wilson of 15 South Sea Road in Cornwall, and the details are that our village was extensively flooded 2 months ago. The entire ground floor of our cottage was submerged in water and five of us have been living in a caravan ever since. You people are still withholding the money we are entitled to over a bizarre technical detail. And it's not acceptable, Paul!
transcript.zh: W: 我是康沃尔郡南海路15号的梅·威尔逊女士。事情是这样的：两个月前，我们的村子遭遇了严重洪水。我们小屋的整个底层都被水淹没了，我们五个人从那以后一直住在一辆拖车里。你们还在因为一个荒唐的技术细节，扣着我们应得的赔款不肯支付。这不可接受，保罗！

transcript.en: M: Miss Wilson, according to the notes on your account, the bizarre technical detail that you mentioned refers to the fact that you hadn't paid house insurance the month before the incident.
transcript.zh: M: 威尔逊女士，根据您账户上的记录，您提到的那个荒唐的技术细节，是指在事故发生前的那个月，您没有支付房屋保险费。

transcript.en: W: That money left our account, and now that you should be paying out, you're suddenly saying that you didn't receive it on time. I'm really skeptical about this claim.
transcript.zh: W: 那笔钱已经从我们的账户里扣走了，而现在到了你们该赔付的时候，你们却突然说没有及时收到这笔钱。我真的对这次理赔感到怀疑。

transcript.en: M: The contract does say that any missed payment in a year will affect the terms and conditions of the insurance contract and may affect claims. Of course, I can pass you on to my manager to talk to you more about this.
transcript.zh: M: 合同确实规定，一年中任何一次漏缴都会影响保险合同的条款和条件，并可能影响理赔。当然，我可以把电话转给我的经理，让他就此事与您进一步沟通。

transcript.en: W: I've already spoken to him, and you can tell him I'm furious now, and that your company has a lawsuit on its hands. You will be hearing from my lawyer. Goodbye.
transcript.zh: W: 我已经和他谈过了，你可以告诉他，我现在非常愤怒，而且你们公司马上就要面临一场诉讼了。你们会收到我律师的通知。再见。

transcript.en: To achieve financial security, how much you save is always more important than the amount you earn or how shrewdly you invest. If you are under 30 years old, your goal should be to save 20% of your monthly income after tax deductions. This is irrespective of how much you earn. Approximately 50% should be reserved for essentials like food and accommodation. The remaining 30% is for recreation and entertainment.
transcript.zh: 要实现财务安全，你储蓄的金额始终比你的收入多少或投资有多精明更为重要。如果你未满30岁，你的目标应当是在扣除税款后，将月收入的20%存下来。这与收入多少无关。大约50%应留作食物和住宿等基本生活开支。剩下的30%用于休闲和娱乐。

transcript.en: But for many young people, it'll be difficult to designate such a large proportion of their income for savings. If you find it hard to save any money at all, start by cutting all unnecessary spending. Allocate a tiny amount of 1 or 2 percent for savings, and gradually increase that amount. Always keep that 20% goal in mind to prevent yourself from becoming complacent. It can be challenging to stick to such a strict plan, but if you adopt the right mindset, you should be able to make it work for you.
transcript.zh: 但是，对许多年轻人来说，将如此大比例的收入用于储蓄会很困难。如果你发现自己连一点钱都很难存下来，就先从削减所有不必要的开支开始。拿出一小部分收入，也就是1%或2%，用于储蓄，然后逐步提高这一比例。始终牢记20%的目标，以免自己变得安于现状。坚持这样严格的计划可能颇具挑战，但如果你采取正确的心态，就应该能够让它为你发挥作用。

transcript.en: So, what should you be doing with the money that you're saving? Some must be kept easily accessible in case you need some cash in an emergency. The largest proportion should be invested in retirement plans, either through your employer or privately. And you can keep some money for high-risk but potentially lucrative investments. Dividends can be reinvested or used to purchase something you like. By following this plan, you should hopefully be able to enjoy your life now, and still be financially secure in the future.
transcript.zh: 那么，你应该如何使用正在储蓄的钱呢？其中一部分必须放在容易取用的地方，以备紧急情况下需要现金。最大的一部分应当投资于退休计划，可以通过雇主进行，也可以自行投资。你还可以留出一部分资金，用于高风险但可能带来丰厚收益的投资。股息可以再投资，也可以用来购买你喜欢的东西。遵循这一计划，你应该有望既享受当下的生活，又在未来保持财务安全。

transcript.en: I work in advertising and I like to keep up with current trends, mainly because I'm aware that we live in an image-obsessed world. However, when I first started my job, occasionally I'd catch a glimpse of myself in the lifts, and find myself thinking that I looked a total mess. Was I being held back by my choice of clothing? The short answer is yes, especially when clients are quick to judge you on your style rather than your work.
transcript.zh: 我从事广告行业，喜欢跟上当前的潮流，主要是因为我意识到我们生活在一个痴迷于外表的世界里。不过，刚开始工作时，我偶尔会在电梯里瞥见自己，然后发现自己觉得自己看起来一团糟。我的着装选择是否阻碍了我的发展？简短的答案是“是”，尤其是当客户很快就会根据你的风格而不是你的工作来评判你时。

transcript.en: But no one can be unique with their outfit every day. I mean, that's why uniforms were invented. So, here's what I did. I created my own uniform. To do this, I chose an appropriate outfit. Then I bought multiple items of the same style in different shades. Now, I never worry about what I'm wearing in the morning even if I do get a bit tired of just wearing the same classic pieces.
transcript.zh: 但是，没有人能每天都穿出与众不同的服装。我的意思是，这就是制服被发明出来的原因。所以，我采取了这样的做法：我为自己设计了一套制服。为此，我选择了一套合适的服装，然后购买了多件不同色调的同款服饰。现在，我早上再也不用担心该穿什么了，尽管总是穿同样的经典款式确实会让我有些厌倦。

transcript.en: Overall, when it comes to work, you have to ask yourself: will looking smarter enhance my ability to do my job? For some, this question may not be an issue at all. Especially if you work remotely and rarely see your colleagues or clients face to face. But if your job involves interacting with other people, the answer to this is often yes. So rather than fighting the system, I think we should just do whatever helps us to achieve our goals at work. If that means playing it safe with your image, then let's face it. It's probably worth it.
transcript.zh: 总的来说，说到工作，你必须问问自己：看起来更得体会增强我的工作能力吗？对有些人来说，这个问题根本不成问题，尤其是当你远程工作，很少与同事或客户面对面交流时。但如果你的工作需要与他人互动，答案通常是肯定的。所以，我认为，与其对抗这种规则，不如做一切有助于我们在工作中实现目标的事情。如果这意味着在外表上采取稳妥的做法，那我们就面对现实吧。这可能是值得的。

transcript.en: Did you know that Americans have approximately three times the amount of space we had 50 years ago? Therefore, you'd think we'd have sufficient room for all of our possessions. On the contrary, the personal storage business is now a growing industry. We've got triple the space, but we've become such enthusiastic consumers that we require even more. This phenomenon has resulted in significant credit card debt, enormous environmental footprints, and perhaps not coincidentally, our happiness levels have failed to increase over the same half century.
transcript.zh: 你知道吗，美国人如今拥有的空间大约是50年前的三倍。因此，你可能会认为，我们应该有足够的空间容纳所有个人物品。然而事实恰恰相反，个人储物业务如今正成为一个不断发展的行业。我们的空间增加了三倍，但我们已经成了如此热衷消费的人，以至于还需要更多空间。这一现象导致了严重的信用卡债务和巨大的环境足迹，而且或许并非巧合，在这半个世纪里，我们的幸福感并没有随之提升。

transcript.en: I'm here to suggest an alternative: having less might actually be a preferable decision. Many of us have experienced, at some stage, the pleasure of possessing less. I propose that less stuff and less space can not only help you economize, but also simplify your life.
transcript.zh: 我想在此提出另一种选择：拥有更少的东西实际上可能是更好的决定。我们中的许多人都曾在人生的某个阶段体验过拥有更少物品所带来的快乐。我认为，减少物品和空间不仅能帮助你节省开支，还能简化你的生活。

transcript.en: I recently started an innovative project to discover some creative solutions that offered me everything I required. By purchasing an apartment that was 40 square meters instead of 60, I immediately saved $200,000. Smaller space leads to reduced utility bills, and also a smaller carbon footprint. Because it is designed around an edited collection of possessions, limited to my favorite stuff, I'm really excited to live there.
transcript.zh: 最近，我启动了一个创新项目，旨在寻找一些能满足我全部需求的创意解决方案。我购买了一套40平方米而不是60平方米的公寓，立即节省了20万美元。空间更小意味着更低的水电费，也意味着更小的碳足迹。由于这套公寓是围绕一组经过筛选、仅限于我最喜爱物品的收藏来设计的，我非常期待住在那里。

transcript.en: How can we live more basically? Firstly, we must ruthlessly cut the unnecessary objects out of our lives. To stem consumption, we should think before we buy, and ask ourselves, "Will it truly make me happier?" Obviously, we should possess some great stuff, but we want belongings that we're going to love for years.
transcript.zh: 我们怎样才能过得更加简朴？首先，我们必须毫不留情地从生活中剔除不必要的物品。为了遏制消费，我们应该在购买之前先思考，并问自己：“它真的会让我更快乐吗？”当然，我们应该拥有一些很棒的物品，但我们希望拥有的是那些我们会喜爱多年的东西。

transcript.en: Secondly, we require space efficiency. We want appliances that are designed for use most of the time, not for occasional use. Why own a six-burner stove when you rarely use even three burners?
transcript.zh: 其次，我们需要提高空间利用效率。我们想要的是那些为大多数时间的使用而设计的电器，而不是只供偶尔使用的电器。既然你连三个炉头都很少同时使用，为什么还要拥有一台六炉头的炉灶呢？

transcript.en: Finally, we need multifunctional spaces and housewares. I combined a movable wall with transforming furniture to get more out of my limited space. Consider my coffee table. It increases in size to accommodate ten. My office is tucked away, easily hidden. My bed simply pops out of the wall. For guests, I can relocate the movable wall and utilize the foldable guest beds I installed.
transcript.zh: 最后，我们需要多功能空间和家居用品。我把一面可移动的墙与可变形家具结合起来，以便更充分地利用有限的空间。以我的咖啡桌为例，它可以扩大，以容纳十个人。我的办公室收纳在隐蔽处，可以轻松藏起来。我的床只需从墙里弹出即可。来客人时，我可以移动那面墙，并使用我安装好的折叠式客床。

transcript.en: I'm not saying we should all live in tiny apartments, but consider the benefits of an edited life. When you return home and walk through your front door, take a moment to ask yourselves, "Could I do with a little life editing? Would that give me more freedom and more time?"
transcript.zh: 我并不是说我们都应该住在小公寓里，但请想一想精简生活的好处。当你回到家，走过前门时，花一点时间问问自己：“我是否可以对生活做些删减？这样会不会让我拥有更多自由和时间？”

transcript.en: Now, believe it or not, people sometimes lie in order to maintain a good, honest reputation—even if it hurts them to do so. At least, this is what a team of scientists is suggesting, with evidence to prove it.
transcript.zh: 信不信由你，人们有时会为了维护良好、诚实的声誉而撒谎，即使这样做会让他们蒙受损失。至少，一组科学家提出了这一观点，并且有证据支持他们的说法。

transcript.en: Picture this scenario: You often drive for work and can be compensated for up to 400 miles per month. Most people at your company drive about 300 miles each month. But this month, you drove 400 miles. How many miles do you think you'd claim in your expense report?
transcript.zh: 设想一下这种情形：你经常因工作需要开车，每月最多可以报销400英里的里程。你所在公司的大多数人每月开车约300英里。但这个月，你开了400英里。你认为自己会在费用报销单上申报多少英里？

transcript.en: The scientists asked this exact question as part of the study we're discussing today. With surprising results, they found that 12% of respondents reported the distance they drove as less than the actual figure, giving an average answer of 384 miles. In other words, they lied about the number of miles, even though they would forfeit money they were owed.
transcript.zh: 作为我们今天要讨论的这项研究的一部分，科学家们提出了这个一模一样的问题。结果令人惊讶：他们发现，12%的受访者报告的驾驶距离低于实际数值，平均回答为384英里。换句话说，他们谎报了驾驶里程，尽管这意味着他们会放弃本应得到的钱。

transcript.en: The researchers believe this was to seem honest, with the assumption being that others would be suspicious of a high expense claim. But why would people fabricate numbers to their own detriment? The researchers explain that many people care a great deal about their reputation and how they'll be judged by others. If they care enough, their concern about appearing honest and not losing the respect of others may be greater than their desire to actually be honest.
transcript.zh: 研究人员认为，这样做是为了显得诚实，因为他们假定别人会对高额费用申报产生怀疑。但人们为什么要捏造数字，让自己蒙受损失呢？研究人员解释说，许多人非常在意自己的声誉，以及别人会如何评价自己。如果这种在意程度足够高，那么他们对显得诚实以及不失去他人尊重的担忧，可能会超过他们真正做到诚实的愿望。

transcript.en: The researchers assert that the findings suggest that when people obtain very favorable outcomes, they anticipate other people's suspicious reactions and prefer lying and appearing honest to telling the truth and appearing as selfish liars.
transcript.zh: 研究人员断言，这些研究结果表明，当人们获得非常有利的结果时，他们会预料到他人产生怀疑的反应，并且更愿意撒谎、装作诚实，也不愿意说出真相、显得像自私的骗子。

transcript.en: So why is this research important? Well, experts generally agree there are two main types of lie-selfish lies and lies that are meant to benefit others. The first, as you may predict, is for selfish gain, such as submitting a fraudulent claim to an insurance company, while the second involves lying to help others or not offend others, for example, telling a friend whose outfit you don't like that they look great.
transcript.zh: 那么，这项研究为什么重要呢？一般来说，专家们认为谎言主要有两种类型：自私的谎言，以及旨在让他人受益的谎言。第一种，正如你可能预料的那样，是为了谋取私利，例如向保险公司提交欺诈性索赔；第二种则是为了帮助他人或不冒犯他人而撒谎，例如告诉一个你不喜欢其穿着的朋友，他们看起来很棒。

transcript.en: But the researchers are suggesting a third type of lying—lying to maintain a good reputation. Now this hypothesis is new and some skeptics argue that this isn't a whole new category of lie.
transcript.zh: 但研究人员提出了第三种撒谎类型，即为了维护良好声誉而撒谎。这个假设是新的，一些怀疑论者认为，这并不是一种全新的谎言类别。

transcript.en: But the findings seem intuitive to me. After all, one of the main motivations for lying is to increase our worth in the eyes of others. So it seems highly likely that people will lie to seem honest.
transcript.zh: 但在我看来，这些研究结果似乎很符合直觉。毕竟，撒谎的主要动机之一，就是提升自己在他人眼中的价值。因此，人们很可能会为了显得诚实而撒谎。

transcript.en: Why do old people dislike new music? As I've grown older, I often hear people my age say things like "They just don't make good music like they used to". Why does this happen? Luckily, psychology can give us some insights into this puzzle. Musical tastes begin to crystallize as early as age 13 or 14. By the time we're in our early 20s, these tastes get locked into place pretty firmly.
transcript.zh: 为什么老年人不喜欢新音乐？随着年龄增长，我经常听到和我年龄相仿的人说：“现在的音乐就是没有过去的好听。”为什么会这样？幸运的是，心理学可以为这个谜题提供一些见解。音乐品味早在十三四岁时就开始逐渐定型。到了二十岁出头，这些品味通常已经相当牢固地固定下来。

transcript.en: In fact, studies have found that by the time we turn 33, most of us have stopped listening to new music. Meanwhile, popular songs released when you're in your early teens are likely to remain quite popular among your age group through the rest of your life.
transcript.zh: 事实上，研究发现，到我们三十三岁时，大多数人已经不再听新音乐了。与此同时，在你十几岁早期发行的流行歌曲，很可能会在你的年龄群体中一直保持相当高的人气，直至你一生的余下时光。

transcript.en: There could be a biological explanation for this, as there's evidence that the brain's ability to make subtle distinctions between different chords, rhythms and melodies deteriorates with age. So to older people, newer, less familiar songs might all "sound the same".
transcript.zh: 对此可能存在一种生物学上的解释，因为有证据表明，随着年龄增长，大脑区分不同和弦、节奏和旋律之间细微差别的能力会逐渐衰退。因此，对老年人来说，较新且不太熟悉的歌曲可能听起来都“一个样”。

transcript.en: But there may be some simpler reasons for older people's aversion to newer music. One of the most researched laws of social psychology is something called the "mere exposure effect", which, in essence, means that the more we're exposed to something, the more we tend to like it. This happens with people we know, the advertisements we see and the songs we listen to.
transcript.zh: 但老年人排斥新音乐也可能有一些更简单的原因。社会心理学中研究最充分的规律之一被称为“纯粹接触效应”，其本质是，我们接触某种事物越多，就越倾向于喜欢它。我们对熟悉的人、所看到的广告以及所听的歌曲，都会产生这种效应。

transcript.en: When you're in your early teens, you probably spend a fair amount of time listening to music or watching music videos. Your favorite songs and artists become familiar, comforting parts of your routine.
transcript.zh: 十几岁早期时，你可能会花相当多的时间听音乐或看音乐视频。你喜欢的歌曲和音乐人会逐渐成为日常生活中熟悉而令人感到安心的一部分。

transcript.en: For many people over 30, job and family obligations increase, so there's less time to spend discovering new music. Instead, many will simply listen to old, familiar favorites from that period of their lives when they had more free time.
transcript.zh: 对许多三十岁以上的人来说，工作和家庭责任增加了，因此用于发现新音乐的时间减少了。相反，许多人会一直听那些熟悉的老歌，那些歌曲来自他们人生中拥有更多空闲时间的时期。

transcript.en: Of course, those teen years weren't necessarily carefree. They're famously confusing, which is why so many TV shows and movies revolve around high school turmoil.
transcript.zh: 当然，青少年时期并不一定无忧无虑。这个阶段出了名地充满困惑，这也是为什么那么多电视节目和电影都围绕高中生活中的动荡展开。

transcript.en: Psychology research has shown that the emotions that we experience as teens seem more intense than those that come later. And we also know that intense emotions are associated with stronger memories and preferences. Both of these might explain why the songs we listen to during this period become so memorable and beloved.
transcript.zh: 心理学研究表明，我们在青少年时期体验到的情绪似乎比后来经历的情绪更加强烈。我们也知道，强烈的情绪与更深刻的记忆和更强烈的偏好有关。这两点都可能解释了为什么我们在这一时期听过的歌曲会变得如此令人难忘，并深受喜爱。

transcript.en: So there's nothing wrong with your parents because they don't like your music. Rather it's all part of the natural order of things.
transcript.zh: 所以，你的父母不喜欢你听的音乐，并不意味着他们有什么问题。这只是事物自然规律的一部分。

matching.title: Why Lifelong Learning Is the International Passport to Success

paragraphs.t: Picture yourself at a college graduation day, with a fresh cohort(一群) of students about to set sail for new horizons. What are they thinking while they throw their caps in the air? What is it with this thin sheet of paper that makes it so precious? It's not only the proof of acquired knowledge but plays into the reputation game of where you were trained. Being a graduate from Harvard Law School carries that extra glamour, doesn't it? Yet take a closer look, and the diploma is the perfect ending to the modern tragedy of education.

Why? Because universities and curricula are designed along the three unities of French classical tragedy: time, action, and place. Students meet at the university campus (unity of place) for classes (unity of action) during their 20s (unity of time). This classical model has traditionally produced prestigious universities, but it is now challenged by the digitalisation of society—which allows everybody who is connected to the internet to access learning—and by the need to acquire skills in step with a fast-changing world. Universities must realise that learning in your 20s won't be enough. If technological diffusion and implementation develop faster, workers will have to constantly refresh their skills.

The university model needs to evolve. It must equip students with the right skills and knowledge to compete in a world 'where value will be derived largely from human interaction and the ability to invent and interpret things that machines cannot', as the English futurist Richard Watson puts it. By teaching foundational knowledge and up-to-date skills, universities will provide students with the future-proof skills of lifelong learning, not just get them 'job-ready'.

Some universities already play a critical role in lifelong learning as they want to keep the value of their diplomas. This new role comes with a huge set of challenges, and needs largely to be invented. One way to start this transformation process could be to go beyond the 'five-year diploma model' to adapt curricula to lifelong learning. We call this model the lifelong passport.

The Bachelor's degree could be your passport to lifelong learning. For the first few years, students would 'learn to learn' and get endowed with reasoning skills that remain with them for the rest of their lives. For instance, physics allows you to observe and rationalise the world, but also to integrate observations into models and, sometimes, models into theories or laws that can be used to make predictions. Mathematics is the language used to formulate the laws of physics or economy, and to make rigorous computations that turn into predictions. These two disciplines naturally form the foundational pillars of education in technical universities.

Recent advances in computational methods and data science push us into rethinking science and engineering. Computers increasingly become principal actors in leveraging data to formulate questions, which requires radically new ways of reasoning. Therefore, a new discipline blending computer science, programming, statistics and machine learning should be added to the traditional foundational topics of mathematics and physics. These three pillars would allow you to keep learning complex technical subjects all your life because numeracy(计算) is the foundation upon which everything else is eventually built.

According to this new model, the Master of Science (MSc) would become the first stamp in the lifelong learning journey. The MSc curriculum should prepare students for their professional career by allowing them to focus on acquiring practical skills through projects.

Those projects are then interwoven with fast-paced technical modules(模块) learned 'on-the-fly' and 'at will' depending on the nature of the project. If, for instance, your project is developing an integrated circuit, you will have to take a module on advanced concepts in microelectronics. The most critical skills will be developed before the project even starts, in the form of boot camps(短期强化训练), while the rest can be fostered along with the project, putting them to immediate use and thus providing a rich learning context.

In addition to technical capabilities, the very nature of projects develops social and entrepreneurial skills, such as design thinking, initiative taking, team leading, activity reporting or resource planning. Not only will those skills be actually integrated into the curriculum but they will be very important to have in the future because they are difficult to automate.

After the MSc diploma is earned, there would be many more stamps of lifelong learning over the years. If universities decide to engage in this learning model, they will have to cope with many organisational challenges that might shake their unity of place and action. First, the number of students would be unpredictable. If all of a university's alumni(往届毕业生) were to become students again, the student body would be much bigger than it is now, and it could become unsustainable for the campus in terms of both size and resources. Second, freshly graduated students would mix with professionally experienced ones. This would change the classroom dynamics, perhaps for the best. Project-based learning with a mixed team reflects the reality of the professional world and could therefore be a better preparation for it.

Sound like science fiction? In many countries, part-time studying is not exceptional: on average across OECD countries, part-time students in 2016 represented 20 per cent of enrolment in tertiary education. In many countries, this share is higher and can exceed 40 per cent in Australia, New Zealand and Sweden.

If lifelong learning were to become a priority and the new norm, diplomas, just like passports, could be revalidated periodically. A time-determined revalidation would ease administration for everybody. Universities as well as employers and employees would know when they have to retrain. For instance, graduates from the year 2000 would have to come back in 2005.

This could fix the main organisational challenges for the university, but not for the learners, due to lack of time, family obligations or funds. Here, online learning might be an option because it allows you to save your 'travel time', but it has its limits. So far, none of the major employers associated with online learning platforms such as Coursera and Udacity has committed to hire or even interview graduates of their new online programmes.

Even if time were not an issue, who will pay for lifelong learning? That's the eternal debate: should it be the learner's responsibility, that of his employer, or of the state? For example, in Massachusetts, the healthcare professions require continuing education credits, which are carefully evidenced and documented. Yet the same state's lawyers don't require continuing legal education, although most lawyers do participate in it informally. One explanation is that technology is less of a factor in law than it is in healthcare.

Europe has many scenarios, but the French and Swiss ones are interesting to compare. In France, every individual has a right to lifelong learning organised via a personal learning account that is credited as you work. In Switzerland, lifelong learning is a personal responsibility and not a government one. However, employers and the state encourage continuing education either by funding parts of it or by allowing employees to attend it.

Universities have a fundamental role to play in this journey, and higher education is in for a change. Just like classical theatre, the old university model produced talent and value for society. We are not advocating its abolition but rather calling for the adaptation of its characteristics to meet the needs of today.

careful.passage: Why does social media trigger feelings of loneliness and inadequacy? Because instead of being real life, it is, for the most part, impression management, a way of marketing yourself, carefully choosing and filtering the pictures and words to put your best face forward. Online "friends" made through social media do not follow the normal psychological progression of an interpersonal relationship. You share neither physical time nor emotional conversations over the Internet. You simply communicate photographs and catchy posts to a diverse group of people whom you have "friended" or "followed" based on an accidental interaction. This is not to say that your social media friends can't be real friends. They absolutely can, but the two are not synonymous. Generally speaking, there are no unfiltered comments or casually taken photos on our social media pages. And, rightfully so, because it wouldn't feel safe to be completely authentic and vulnerable with some of our "friends" whom we don't actually know or with whom trust has yet to be built. Social media can certainly be an escape from the daily grind, but we must be cautioned against the negative effects, such as addiction, on a person's overall psychological well-being. As humans, we yearn for social connection. Scrolling( 滚动) through pages of pictures and comments, however, does not provide the same degree of fulfillment as face-to-face interactions do. Also, we tend to idealize others' lives and compare our downfalls to their greatest accomplishments, ending in feelings of loneliness and inadequacy. Social media can lead people on the unhealthy quest for perfection. Some people begin to attend certain events or travel to different places so that they can snap that "perfect" photo. They begin to seek validation through the number of people who "like" their posts. In order for it to play a psychologically healthy role in your social life, social media should supplement an already healthy social network. Pictures and posts should be byproducts of life's treasured moments and fun times, not the planned and calculated image that one is putting out into cyberspace in an attempt to fill insecurities or unmet needs. Ultimately, social media has increased our ability to connect with various types of people all over the globe. It has opened doors for businesses and allowed us to stay connected to people whom we may not otherwise get to follow. However, social media should feel like a fun experience, not one that contributes to negative thoughts and feelings. If the latter is the case, increasing face-to-face time with trusted friends, and minimizing time scrolling online, will prove to be a reminder that your social network is much more rewarding than any "like," "follow" or "share" can be.

careful.passage: Imagine that an alien species landed on Earth and, through their mere presence, those aliens caused our art to vanish, our music to homogenize, and our technological know-how to disappear. That is effectively what humans have been doing to our closest relatives—chimps(大猩猩). Back in 1999, a team of scientists led by Andrew Whiten showed that chimps from different parts of Africa behave very differently from one another. Some groups would get each other's attention by rapping branches with their knuckles(指关节), while others did it by loudly ripping leaves with their teeth. The team identified 39 of these traditions that are practiced by some communities but not others—a pattern that, at the time, hadn't been seen in any animal except humans. It was evidence, the team said, that chimps have their own cultures. It took a long time to convince skeptics that such cultures exist, but now we have plenty of examples of animals learning local traditions from one another. But just when many scientists have come to accept the existence of animal cultures, many of those cultures might vanish. Ammie Kalan and her colleagues have shown, through years of intensive fieldwork, that the very presence of humans has eroded the diversity of chimp behavior. Where we flourish, their cultures wither. It is a bitterly ironic thing to learn on the 20th anniversary of Whiten's classic study. "It's amazing to think that just 60 years ago, we knew next to nothing of the behavior of our sister species in the wild," Whiten says. "But now, just as we are truly getting to know our primate(灵长类) cousins, the actions of humans are closing the window on all we have discovered." "Sometimes in the rush to conserve the species, I think we forget about the individuals," says Cat Hobaiter, a professor at the University of St. Andrews. "Each population, each community, even each generation of chimps is unique. An event might only have a small impact on the total population of chimps, but it may wipe out an entire community—an entire culture. No matter what we do to restore habitat or support population growth, we may never be able to restore that culture." No one knows whether the destruction of chimp culture is getting worse. Few places have tracked chimp behavior over long periods, and those that have are also more likely to have protected their animals from human influence. Obviously, conservationists need to think about saving species in a completely new way—by preserving animal traditions as well as bodies and genes. "Instead of focusing only on the conservation of genetically based entities like species, we now need to also consider culturally based entities," says Andrew Whiten.

translation.source: 北京大兴国际机场位于天安门广场以南46公里处，于2019年9月30日投入使用。该巨型工程于2014年开工 建设，高峰时工地上有4万多工人。航站楼设计紧凑，可以允许最大数量的飞机直接停靠在最靠近航站楼中心 的位置，这给乘客提供了极大的方便。航站楼共有82个登机口，但乘客通过安检后，只需不到8分钟就能抵达 任何一个登机口。机场的设计可确保每小时300架次起降。机场年客运量2040年将达到1亿人次，有望成为世界 上最繁忙的机场。
translation.reference: Located 46 kilometers south of Tian'anmen Square, Beijing Daxing International Airport was put into use on September 30, 2019. Construction of this massive project began in 2014, and at the peak there were more than 40,000 workers on the construction site. The compact design of the terminal allows the maximum number of aircraft to dock directly at the positions closest to its center, which provides great convenience for passengers. The terminal has 82 boarding gates in total, but after passing through security check, passengers can reach any gate in less than 8 minutes. The design of the airport ensures 300 takeoffs and landings per hour. The airport's annual passenger volume is expected to reach 100 million by 2040, and it is likely to become the busiest airport in the world.
